transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~75 minutes
Attendees: Ari Patel (Redwood AE), Sofia Chen (Redwood SE), Diego Morales (Redwood), Lena Ortiz (HorizonAI), Markus Klein (HorizonAI), Priya Das (HorizonAI), Evan Wu (HorizonAI)

-- Auto-generated summary (optional) --
Ari: quick intro, goals: understand perf differences between TRT-LLM and vLLM, validate kernel selection paths and whether CUDA graphs help our 1-2 token latency tight workloads.

[00:00] Ari Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick agenda: kernel selection, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM comparisons, CUDA graphs behavior, KV cache and batching patterns, and quantization options. We should end with clear next steps.
[00:18] Priya Das: Thanks Ari, high level: HorizonAI runs a mix of short chat completions and docs summarization, latency 99 P95 targets around 120ms for 128-token contexts is ideal for product. We also have some on-prem pockets with NVLink-connected A100s.
[00:35] Sofia Chen: Got it. we'll focus on both throughput and tail latency. quick clarification — when you say 128-token context, do you mean 128 input + generated tokens?
[00:45] Lena Ortiz: Mostly input ~64 and generation up to 128, so total sequence can hit 192 in long tails, but typical is 64->80. we care about cold-start and steady-state latencies.
[01:05] Markus Klein: also, note our on-prem infra uses Mellanox 200Gb NICs and NVLink across 2xA100s; we can't necessarily shard easily across racks due to security zones.

[01:30] Diego Morales: Quick note on kernel selection: Redwood's runtime uses a heuristics table that picks from several kernels (cuBLAS/fused attention, FlashAttention variants, TensorRT fused kernels) based on seq len, batch size, head size. For TRT-LLM we often prefer fused TRT attention at longer sequence lengths because of memory-bandwidth advantages.
[01:55] Sophia (typo in transcript)
[02:00] Sofia Chen: sorry, Sofia here — sometimes the transcribe flips my name — the important bit is that kernel choice depends heavily on sequence distribution and kv-cache hit patterns. If you have warm KV cache and shorter incremental tokens, the overhead of launching different kernels dominates.
[02:20] Lena Ortiz: that's interesting — can you quantify? like where does TRT win vs vLLM?
[02:35] Sofia Chen: From our internal benchmarks: for batch sizes >=8 and sequence lengths >256, TensorRT-LLM tends to have 10-30% better throughput. For single-shot low-batch (<4) with many small incremental tokens, vLLM's continuous batching and lower kernel-launch overhead often gives lower tail latency. But there are many caveats — quantization and CUDA graphs change the story.
[03:10] Evan Wu: we run a high-variance workload — lots of short chats and some bulk ingests. tail is critical.

[03:30] Ari Patel: let's talk CUDA graphs. Sofia?
[03:35] Sofia Chen: sure. CUDA graphs reduce per-inference kernel launch overhead by capturing the exec graph. For predictable sequences they are great — we saw up to 2-4x reduction in CPU overhead and 15-25% lower P99 in some configs. But caveats: graphs are sensitive to input shapes and dynamic KV size. If your incremental token length varies a lot, you need multiple graphs or fallback which complicates memory planning. Also TRT engines with graphs may need re-capture when attention mask shapes change.
[04:20] Lena Ortiz: so for our short-chat workload with variable gen length, are graphs still worth it?
[04:35] Sofia Chen: likely yes for the hot path: precompute graphs for the most common token increments — e.g., 1, 4, 8 tokens — and fall back to dynamic path for uncommon sizes. That gives most of the benefit while keeping correctness. One more thing: graphs + KV cache plays nice if KV lives on GPU and you're careful with memory offsets. If KV has to be reallocated or evicted, you lose the benefit.
[05:05] Markus Klein: what about kernel selection when using 4-bit quant?
[05:12] Sofia Chen: quantization changes compute patterns. INT8/4-bit kernels (and quantized matmul kernels) can be faster and reduce memory enough to do larger batches on a single GPU. But some fused attention kernels aren't fully quantized yet, so runtime will choose different paths — sometimes falling back to non-fused kernels which hurts latency. For production we recommend running end-to-end A/B with your prompts; we can run accuracy regressions on the prompt set.
[06:00] Priya Das: can you share examples of the perf numbers? rough ballpark.
[06:10] Sofia Chen: sure, rough numbers from our lab on A100 40GB:
- vLLM: single client, batch=1, 64->64 (total 128): P95 ~140ms, P99 ~220ms
- TRT-LLM (FP16 + engine): batch=1 same shape: P95 ~120ms, P99 ~190ms
- TRT-LLM with CUDA graphs (hot path capture): P95 ~100ms, P99 ~150-160ms
- vLLM heavy continuous batching (many small clients aggregated): throughput higher and cost per token lower for bursty multi-client workloads
(These are illustrative; your NVLink topology and NICs will change numbers)
[07:05] Lena Ortiz: those numbers look promising. curious about KV-cache eviction policy — our prompts sometimes change context, we can't keep very long KV cache per session.
[07:20] Sofia Chen: Redwood supports prefix caching and per-customer cache sizing. We expose eviction metrics and recommend TTL-based eviction for short sessions and LRU for longer. Important is to colocate KV with the runtime to avoid PCIe transfers; on Dedicated you can keep KV fully GPU resident. On Private/on-prem, that depends on your memory footprint and whether you pin pages with NVLink.
[07:55] Markus Klein: on our on-prem, memory is the constraint — we often can't keep the full KV for 4 concurrent sessions at 192 tokens each. what are strategies?
[08:10] Diego Morales: two approaches: 1) shard sessions across GPUs with smaller KV per GPU or 2) quantize KV to 4-bit w/ accuracy checks. Also use selective prefix caching: only cache the most recent N tokens or most frequent prefixes. We have tooling to simulate hit rates given your workload traces.
[08:45] Priya Das: how about multi-GPU scaling? TRT-LLM engine supports model parallel?
[08:55] Sofia Chen: TRT-LLM is focused on single-GPU engine performance; for model parallel we use a combination of tensor-slicing and pipeline parallelism. vLLM has more flexible scheduler for multi-GPU batching scenarios. For HorizonAI's constraints (NVLink across 2xA100s) we can either fit a quantized model single-GPU or split with NCCL-based topologies. We'll need to test both.

[09:30] Ari Patel: any gotchas with CUDA graphs + dynamic attention masks?
[09:35] Sofia Chen: yes — masks change shapes and that invalidates graphs. Workarounds: capture graph per typical mask shapes or use masked-padded fixed-size graphs with extra no-op work to absorb variance. This increases memory but preserves graph reuse. Also watch out for stream synchronization when mixing graphs and dynamic kernels.
[10:10] Evan Wu: what about prefill vs incremental timing — like cold-start when the cache is empty?
[10:16] Sofia Chen: cold-start costs more because KV must be written and cublas/TensorRT engines must warm up. We recommend warming engines with small synthetic batches during low-traffic windows and prefill common prefixes. With graphs you can also pre-capture the prefill path. This reduces first-token latency substantially.

[10:50] Lena Ortiz: for quantization — how often do you see quality regressions at 4-bit? Any tools to monitor?
[10:58] Sofia Chen: 4-bit works well for many models but depends on vocab and task. We run per-prompt evals and delta checks; Redwood Optimize can generate candidate quant profiles and run regressions on your eval set. Expect small regressions on instruction-following tasks; some customers use mixed precision (critical layers FP16) to avoid regressions.

[11:40] Markus Klein: networking and VPC: if we deploy Private in our VPC with HSM integration, any performance hits?
[11:48] Ari Patel: generally KMS/HSM doesn't impact per-token latency if keys are used for initial decryption and then session keys are kept in memory, but audit/logging can add overhead to control plane operations. Data-plane latency is mostly local to GPU. For cross-zone traffic, NVLink matters; avoid moving KV over PCIe/ethernet if possible.
[12:15] Priya Das: our security team will ask for SOC2 artifacts and RBAC. Can Redwood provide?
[12:20] Ari Patel: yes — we will share SOC2, ISO attestation links and discuss RBAC/SSO flows. We'll include that in the follow-up security packet.

[12:40] Sofia Chen: Back to benchmarks — operationally we suggest capturing: kernel-selection logs, nvprof/CUDA graph traces, GPU utilization, PCIe copy times, and token-level latency. We'll provide a benchmark harness that runs TRT-LLM and vLLM variants against the same prompt set and spits out delta heatmaps.
[13:10] Lena Ortiz: can you run mixed workloads? we need both streaming chat and bulk embed-type tasks on same pool.
[13:20] Diego Morales: yes we can mix — route by policy: low-latency chat to TRT-LLM engines with reserved capacity; background bulk to shared clusters with batching. Redwood routing can also fallback if capacity constrained.

[13:55] Markus Klein: curious about costs — how big a delta do customers normally see moving from vLLM to TRT-LLM?
[14:00] Sofia Chen: depends on utilization. For high-throughput steady workloads TRT-LLM can reduce GPUs needed by 20-40%. For bursty low-batch real-time chat vLLM continuous batching can have lower cost per token because of aggregation. We'll put cost models in the benchmark report.

[14:35] Ari Patel: let's capture final action items and next steps.
[14:40] Priya Das: quick ask — we need a pilot agreement that includes confidentiality and data residency notes for on-prem sessions.
[14:50] Ari Patel: we'll send the pilot template and security addendum.
[15:00] Sofia Chen: I'll attach the CUDA graphs traces and initial kernel selection logs. Ari will provision sandbox endpoints for your prompt runs.
[15:15] Lena Ortiz: thanks all — this was very helpful.
[15:20] Ari Patel: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the benchmark plan and schedule the review call for next week.

-- End transcript --
